Trust the speaker assignments in the transcript.
Do not trust or use the timestamps for classifying prompts. 
Utterances that are off task can be prompts. 
Most questions will be prompts, but not all e.g., rhetorical questions or questions requesting a behavioral or written response.
Most statements will not be prompts, but some will e.g., calling someone by name.
Behavioral instructions are questions or statements that request a non-verbal action be performed. Behavioral instructions are not classified as prompts. 
Examples of behavioral instructions include, “write down your answer,” “raise your hand,” or “thumbs up” and do not include any verbal component. 
Behavioral instructions can have similar word patterns as dialogic prompts. 
“Tell them” or “talk to your classmates” is a prompt when used to imply a person should begin talking or articulate their thinking. It is not a prompt if it is clearly used only to redirect to whom someone is speaking to, i.e., when used to imply “you should say that to someone else.” 
A request to repeat something is a prompt because it often fosters discussion beyond a sole behavioral instruction 
A request to “try again” is a prompt when the thing they are trying again is a verbal response 
Rhetorical questions are questions asked, “only to produce an effect or make a statement, rather than to elicit an answer or information” (Oxford English Dictionary). Rhetorical questions are not classified as prompts. 
One example of a rhetorical question is, “what?” when used as an exclamation. 
Questions that appear at the beginning of an utterance but are answered within the same utterance are considered rhetorical, and therefore not a prompt. 
If it is unclear whether a question is rhetorical, use other features of the utterance and the context (e.g., whether it was responded to) to determine if it should be classified as a prompt.
